explanation: Horace, Odes 1.11. The verb is really 'pluck', as you would pick fruit: enjoy what is ripe now, because you do not know what tomorrow holds.
A medieval Christian motto, often tied to the story of a slave whispering to a triumphing general. That anecdote is only loosely related. Used to put small worries in perspective.
Suetonius reports it as a favourite saying of Emperor Augustus, translating an older Greek maxim. Speed and care are not opposites; rushing usually costs time.

translation: I came, I saw, I conquered.
explanation: Julius Caesar's report on a lightning victory at Zela in 47 BC, according to Suetonius and Plutarch. The ultimate short status update.
Said by Caesar when crossing the Rubicon in 49 BC, as Suetonius tells it (in the word order 'iacta alea est'). It means a point of no return has been passed.
An old proverb; Pliny the Elder already notes that people say truth is found in wine. Tipsy people talk, and not always wisely.

translation: Art is long, life is short.
explanation: Latin form of the opening of Hippocrates' Aphorisms, where 'art' means the craft of medicine. Mastering anything takes longer than a lifetime allows.
A shortening of Virgil's 'fugit inreparabile tempus' (Georgics 3): irreplaceable time flees. Clocks have borrowed it ever since.

translation: A sound mind in a sound body.
explanation: Juvenal, Satires 10. Often quoted as a fitness slogan, but he says it is one of the few things worth praying for, along with courage.
Juvenal, Satires 10: the Roman people, who once gave out power, now anxiously want only food and shows. Still used for politics that buys applause.

translation: If you want peace, prepare for war.
explanation: A modern short form of a line by the late Roman writer Vegetius. It is the logic of deterrence, and of every arms race.

translation: The voice of the people is the voice of God.
explanation: A medieval saying. Alcuin quoted it in a letter to Charlemagne only to reject it, since crowds are often wrong. Worth remembering at election time.
A legal maxim of sales law: the buyer is responsible for checking what they buy. The seller is not obliged to point out the flaws.

translation: The law is harsh, but it is the law.
explanation: A legal maxim. Rules apply even when the result feels unfair. The answer is to change the law, not to ignore it.
Terence uses it in the Adelphoe for someone who shows up just as he is being discussed. The English cousin is 'speak of the devil'.
Horace, Odes 3.30. He is proud that his poems will outlive him, and he was right: we are still quoting him two thousand years later.
The first words of Catullus's poem 85, two lines long. He cannot explain it, he only feels it, and it hurts. The shortest love poem ever written.
Cicero, Pro Roscio Amerino, credits the Roman judge Cassius with asking it in criminal cases. To understand why something happened, follow the advantage.

translation: Oh the times, oh the customs!
explanation: Cicero, Against Catiline, the opening of his attack on a conspirator in the Senate. The timeless complaint of every generation about the next.
Cicero, Pro Rabirio Postumo. It is a cheerful line, but note the price of the lessons, which is paid in mistakes.
Thomas a Kempis, The Imitation of Christ. You can make all the plans you like. Whatever happens next is not up to you.

translation: A drop hollows out the stone.
explanation: Ovid, Letters from Pontus, which continues 'not by force but by falling often'. Persistence beats strength, given enough time.
Horace, Epistles 1.2. Kant adopted it as the motto of the Enlightenment: have the courage to use your own reason.
Virgil, Aeneid 10. Said by Turnus, who then lost. Fortune favours the bold, but only sometimes, and not for long.

latin: Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto
translation: I am a man; I consider nothing human foreign to me.
pronunciation: HOH-moh soom, hoo-MAH-nee NEE-hil ah meh ah-lee-AY-noom POO-toh
explanation: Terence, Heauton Timorumenos. It is said by a character who is nosy about a neighbour. It became the motto of humanism.
According to Livy, Brennus, the Gallic chief, said it after sacking Rome, throwing his sword on the scale as ransom was weighed. The winner writes the rules.

translation: The world wants to be deceived, so let it be deceived.
explanation: Of uncertain origin, often attributed to Petronius. A cynic's business plan: if people prefer the illusion, sell them the illusion.
Attributed to Emperor Vespasian, who taxed public urinals and held a coin under his son's nose to prove the point (Suetonius). It does not matter where the money comes from.

translation: Who will guard the guards themselves?
explanation: Juvenal, Satires 6, originally about keeping wives faithful. Now used for any power with nobody checking it.

translation: Man is a wolf to man.
explanation: Plautus, Asinaria, where it is said of a stranger you do not know. Hobbes later made it a motto of the state of nature.
From the Vulgate, Psalm 41. Used for how one misfortune, or one mistake, tends to drag the next one behind it.

translation: Laughter abounds in the mouth of fools.
explanation: A medieval proverb. People laugh most loudly at the jokes they understand least.

translation: Now is the time to drink.
explanation: Horace, Odes 1.37, written to celebrate the fall of Cleopatra. It is the Latin for 'let us open the bottle'.

translation: There is no arguing about tastes.
explanation: A scholastic maxim of uncertain origin. It is a polite way of ending a debate in which nobody will change their mind.

translation: Repetition is the mother of learning.
explanation: A traditional school proverb. Nothing sticks without being said, and heard, again.

translation: So great are the evils that religion could persuade people to commit.
explanation: Lucretius, On the Nature of Things 1. He is thinking of the sacrifice of Iphigenia. Written two thousand years ago and still debated.
Horace, Ars Poetica. Even the greatest author has weak passages. It is a kinder verdict than it sounds.

translation: If you had kept quiet, you would have remained a philosopher.
explanation: Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy. A man who has boasted of being a philosopher is mocked once he reacts angrily to an insult. Silence preserves a reputation.
Lucretius, among others, repeating an idea of Greek philosophy. It is the first principle of physics, and of any budget.
Petronius, Satyricon, describes a painted warning of this kind at a rich man's door. Mosaics with the same words survive at Pompeii.
